variants.title: Run the evaluation path
variants.context: The evaluation path runs from versioned cases, through a candidate scorer that is the exact preprocessing, model, threshold, and policy mapping proposed for release, to slice diagnosis, and only then to a bounded rollout with predeclared gates, review capacity, appeals, and rollback.
variants.prompt: A moderation classifier is being prepared for release. Put the evaluation path in order.

items.text: Score them with the exact preprocessing, model, threshold, and policy mapping proposed for release.
Report confusion counts, uncertainty, target-group slices, and functional pass rates.
Grant a bounded rollout with predeclared gates, review capacity, appeals, and rollback ownership.
Assemble versioned cases with provenance, labels, slices, and a protected holdout.

variants.hint: Which artifact has to exist before anything can be scored?
variants.explanation: Versioned cases, the exact candidate scorer, sliced diagnosis, and bounded exposure are separate stages with separate owners.

variants.title: Run the evaluation path
variants.context: The evaluation path runs from versioned cases, through a candidate scorer that is the exact preprocessing, model, threshold, and policy mapping proposed for release, to slice diagnosis, and only then to a bounded rollout with predeclared gates, review capacity, appeals, and rollback.
variants.prompt: A normalization step is added to strip zero-width characters. Put the revalidation in order.

items.text: Decide the rollout, since a preprocessing change can move both harmful misses and benign flags.
Rerun scoring with the new normalization inside the candidate pipeline, not as a separate script.
Pull the frozen case set, including the perturbed and clean-text holdouts.
Compare slice miss rates and functional accuracy before and after the change.

variants.hint: The change belongs inside the scored candidate, not beside it.
variants.explanation: Preprocessing is part of the system under test, so revalidation replays the whole path rather than the model alone.

variants.prompt: An appeal shows benign counter-speech being removed in production. Put the follow-up in order.

items.text: Rescore the suite against the candidate that is currently serving that decision.
Add the de-identified appealed case to the versioned set with its reviewer outcome.
Reset the rollout limit and review capacity to match the corrected operating point.
Break the result out by the counter-speech function and by target-group slice.

variants.hint: An appeal is evidence, so where does it enter the path?
variants.explanation: Confirmed production errors become versioned cases, which is what lets the next scoring run detect the same mistake.

variants.title: Prepare the release evidence
variants.context: Before a release the team freezes the threshold and slice gates on a calibration partition, deduplicates exact and semantic neighbors across partitions, adds product languages and policy cases the public suites do not cover, adjudicates ambiguous cases with trained reviewers, and capacity-tests review, appeals, and rollback at the expected flagged volume.
variants.prompt: A team is a week from a moderation release. Put the preparation steps in order.

items.text: Capacity-test human review, appeals, and rollback at the expected flagged volume.
Add the product's languages, context lengths, and policy boundaries that public suites miss.
Deduplicate exact and semantic neighbors across training, calibration, and release partitions.
Freeze the threshold and slice gates on the calibration partition before the release set is opened.
Adjudicate ambiguous and high-severity cases with trained reviewers and record disagreement.

variants.hint: Which step must happen before anyone can see a release-set score?
variants.explanation: Thresholds are set on calibration data, then the release set stays untouched until it answers whether the candidate met that policy.

variants.prompt: The product is expanding to a second language. Put the preparation steps in order.

items.text: Check the new cases against every existing partition for translated and near-duplicate overlap.
Size review and appeals staffing for the flagged volume the new language will produce.
Have qualified native reviewers adjudicate the contested cases and log their disagreement.
Add product policy cases in that language, including local slurs and reclaimed terms.
Fix the gates for the new language on its own calibration partition first.

variants.hint: A new language needs its own calibration, not the old threshold.
variants.explanation: Public English suites do not establish behavior in another language, so gates, cases, reviewers, and capacity are rebuilt for it.

variants.title: Prepare the release evidence
variants.context: Before a release the team freezes the threshold and slice gates on a calibration partition, deduplicates exact and semantic neighbors across partitions, adds product languages and policy cases the public suites do not cover, adjudicates ambiguous cases with trained reviewers, and capacity-tests review, appeals, and rollback at the expected flagged volume.
variants.prompt: Confirmed incidents from last quarter are being folded into the program. Put the work in order.

items.text: Deduplicate the incident cases against the tuning and prompt-development partitions.
Retest reviewer, appeal, and rollback capacity against the volume those cases imply.
Adjudicate the ambiguous incident labels with trained reviewers rather than reusing the original call.
Declare the gates and threshold on calibration data before the incident cases are scored.
Add the incidents as product-specific cases with their policy context and consequence.

variants.hint: A confirmed incident is protected evidence, not immediate tuning data.
variants.explanation: Incidents become a future protected regression set, which only works if they are deduplicated and adjudicated before they gate anything.

variants.title: Read the confusion counts
variants.context: A moderation gate reads confusion counts with the correct denominator. Harmful recall divides detected harmful cases by all harmful cases, the legitimate false-positive rate divides flagged benign cases by all benign cases, and a slice miss rate uses only the harmful cases inside that slice.
variants.prompt: At the frozen threshold a suite holds 400 harmful and 600 legitimate cases. 336 harmful cases score above the threshold. What is harmful recall in percent?
variants.hint: Which cases belong in the denominator for recall?
variants.explanation: 336 detections over the 400 harmful cases is 84 percent recall; the legitimate cases belong to a different rate.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by all 1,000 cases instead of the 400 harmful ones.
That reports the miss rate rather than recall.

variants.title: Read the confusion counts
variants.context: A moderation gate reads confusion counts with the correct denominator. Harmful recall divides detected harmful cases by all harmful cases, the legitimate false-positive rate divides flagged benign cases by all benign cases, and a slice miss rate uses only the harmful cases inside that slice.
variants.prompt: At the frozen threshold a suite holds 400 harmful and 500 legitimate cases. 60 legitimate cases are flagged as harmful. What is the legitimate false-positive rate in percent?
variants.hint: False positives are counted against the benign population only.
variants.explanation: 60 flagged benign cases over the 500 legitimate cases is a 12 percent false-positive rate.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by all 900 cases instead of the 500 legitimate ones.
That reports the share of legitimate cases correctly left alone.

variants.title: Read the confusion counts
variants.context: A moderation gate reads confusion counts with the correct denominator. Harmful recall divides detected harmful cases by all harmful cases, the legitimate false-positive rate divides flagged benign cases by all benign cases, and a slice miss rate uses only the harmful cases inside that slice.
variants.prompt: A suite holds 300 harmful cases, of which 150 are implicit stereotypes. 48 implicit cases score below the threshold. What is the implicit slice miss rate in percent?
variants.hint: A slice rate uses the slice's own denominator.
variants.explanation: 48 misses over the 150 implicit harmful cases is a 32 percent miss rate for that slice.

mistakes.feedback: That divides the misses by all 300 harmful cases instead of the 150 in the slice.
That reports recall on the slice rather than its miss rate.

variants.title: Diagnose the functional failure
variants.context: HateCheck isolates one linguistic behavior at a time with minimal contrasts. A detector passes a function only when it handles the hateful case and its minimally changed non-hateful contrast, and each functional failure has a specific engineering action rather than a word exception.
variants.prompt: The detector flags 'I hate [GROUP]' and also flags 'I do not hate [GROUP]' at the same score. Which failure is this, and what follows?
options: A negation failure, so inspect context encoding and add held-out negated contrasts.
A spelling-variation miss, so test normalization against clean-text regressions.
A non-protected target overblock, so separate sentiment from group-targeted harm.
optionFeedback: One negation flips the meaning while the decision does not, which is what this function tests.
Nothing was misspelled here; the two cases differ only by the negation.
The target is a protected group in both cases, so this is not a target-scope error.
variants.hint: What single change was made between the two cases?
variants.explanation: A minimal contrast that flips meaning without flipping the decision fails the function, and the fix is context encoding rather than a word exception.

variants.title: Diagnose the functional failure
variants.context: HateCheck isolates one linguistic behavior at a time with minimal contrasts. A detector passes a function only when it handles the hateful case and its minimally changed non-hateful contrast, and each functional failure has a specific engineering action rather than a word exception.
variants.prompt: The detector catches a slur written normally but misses the same slur with inserted spaces and character swaps. Which failure is this, and what follows?
options: A spelling-variation miss, so test normalization and character-aware features.
A counter-speech overblock, so preserve quotation and speech-act context.
A negation failure, so add independently held-out negated contrasts.
optionFeedback: Surface perturbation defeats the decision, which is the perturbation class of tests.
Nothing here is counter-speech; both cases are the same hateful statement.
No negation was introduced, only a change in surface form.
variants.hint: The meaning is unchanged; only the characters moved.
variants.explanation: Perturbation functions test whether surface changes break the decision, and the repair is normalization checked against clean-text regressions.

variants.title: Diagnose the functional failure
variants.context: HateCheck isolates one linguistic behavior at a time with minimal contrasts. A detector passes a function only when it handles the hateful case and its minimally changed non-hateful contrast, and each functional failure has a specific engineering action rather than a word exception.
variants.prompt: The detector flags 'I cannot stand my landlord' as group-targeted hate. Which failure is this, and what follows?
options: A spelling-variation miss, so test normalization and character-aware features.
A negation failure, so inspect how the model encodes negated context.
A non-protected target overblock, so separate negative sentiment from group harm.
optionFeedback: The text is written plainly, so surface perturbation is not what fired here.
There is no negated contrast in this case to explain the decision.
Negative sentiment aimed at a non-protected target is a contrastive non-hate case.
variants.hint: Who is the target, and is that target protected?
variants.explanation: Contrastive non-hate cases fail when the model equates hostility with group-targeted harm, so the two signals have to be separated.

variants.title: Pick the evidence for the claim
variants.context: Each resource answers a different question. ToxiGen asks whether implicit harmful statements separate from benign statements about the same groups, HateCheck asks which linguistic functions the classifier handles, a product suite asks whether that transfers to the deployed policy and languages, and operations ask whether the remaining errors can be contained.
variants.prompt: Match each claim to the resource that can support it.

pairs.label: The detector separates implicit harm from benign mentions of the same groups
pairs.detail: ToxiGen, whose balanced generation reduces the shortcut that treats any identity mention as toxic.

pairs.label: The detector handles negation, counter-speech, and spelling variation
pairs.detail: HateCheck, whose minimal contrasts isolate one linguistic function at a time.

pairs.label: The behavior holds under the product's own policy, languages, and context
pairs.detail: A versioned product challenge set built from governed examples of real traffic.

pairs.label: The errors that remain can still be contained after launch
pairs.detail: Capacity-tested human review, appeals, monitoring, and rollback ownership.

variants.hint: Ask which question each resource was built to answer.
variants.explanation: Breadth, diagnosis, relevance, and containment are four different claims, and no single benchmark supplies more than one.

variants.prompt: Match each claim to the resource that can support it.

pairs.label: Implicit statements without profanity are still detected
pairs.detail: ToxiGen, whose adversarial generation targets subtle examples an existing detector found difficult.

pairs.label: Quoted discussion of a slur is not removed as hate
pairs.detail: HateCheck, whose contrastive non-hateful cases cover quotation and reclaimed terms.

pairs.label: Spanish-language traffic behaves the way the English evidence suggested
pairs.detail: A product challenge set in that language, since the public suites are English and text-only.

pairs.label: Ambiguous and high-severity cases resolve consistently
pairs.detail: Trained human adjudication with documented disagreement and reviewer wellbeing controls.

variants.hint: One of these claims is about a language the public suites never covered.
variants.explanation: A claim is only as strong as the resource that measured it, so the release record names which source carries which sentence.

pairs.label: The threshold does not turn every group mention into a removal
pairs.detail: ToxiGen benign statements about the same 13 groups, scored as their own slice.

pairs.label: Each defined linguistic function has a reported pass rate
pairs.detail: HateCheck functionality-level accuracy, reported per function rather than averaged.

pairs.label: Flagged volume stays inside what reviewers can actually handle
pairs.detail: An operational capacity test at the expected flagged volume before rollout.

pairs.label: Removed posts can be contested and the outcome fed back
pairs.detail: An appeals path whose reversals are monitored by slice after release.

variants.hint: Two of these claims are operational rather than about the model.
variants.explanation: A defensible release needs breadth, functional diagnosis, product evidence, and operational controls for the errors that remain.
